examples|examples-t1|1.3.note: Fiscal 2023 vs 2022: comparable sales (3.2)%, comparable customer transactions (2.9)%, comparable average ticket (0.3)%; customer transactions 1,621.8 million vs 1,666.4 million, (2.7)%; average ticket $90.07 vs $90.36, (0.3)%; excludes HD Supply.
examples|examples-t1|1.3.issues: No real issues. All eight numbers match the table: comparable sales (3.2)%, comparable customer transactions (2.9)%, comparable average ticket (0.3)%, customer transactions 1,621.8M vs 1,666.4M at (2.7)%, and average ticket $90.07 vs $90.36 at (0.3)%. One minor point: footnote (1) excludes HD Supply only from the transaction and average-ticket rows, not from comparable sales. Because "excludes HD Supply" comes at the end of the note, a reader could take it to cover every figure. For the task, the note keeps the split between transactions and ticket for both the comparable and total measures. The piece names no management factors, so nothing is lost there. Leaving out sales per square foot, EPS and fiscal 2021 is fine because they don't bear on the task.

examples|examples-t1|1.4.note: Fiscal 2023 net sales down $4.7 billion, 3.0%, to $152.7 billion. Comparable sales -3.2%: transactions -2.9% (goods-to-services shift, higher interest rates); average ticket -0.3% (commodity deflation ~145 basis points, mainly lumber, partly offset by product inflation, innovative products).
examples|examples-t1|1.4.issues: No material issues. Every number matches the piece: net sales down $4.7 billion (3.0%) to $152.7 billion; comparable sales -3.2%; transactions -2.9%; average ticket -0.3%; commodity deflation of about 145 basis points, driven mainly by lumber. The factors behind each part are correctly assigned. Transactions: the shift from goods to services and higher interest rates. Average ticket: deflation, partly offset by inflation and innovative products. Minor compressions that change no meaning: (1) The piece calls the offsets "demand for new and innovative products"; the note shortens this to "innovative products". (2) The piece's "inflation across several product categories, which slowed relative to prior years" becomes "product inflation" in the note, and the slowing is dropped. (3) The note drops "U.S." from commodity price deflation. (4) It also leaves out the framing that these are "macroeconomic factors ... pressuring home improvement demand". The note also leaves out the online sales share (14.8%, +1.1%), the $276 million boost from a weaker U.S. dollar, and department-level results, including Lumber's double-digit decline. None of these is needed to answer the task's split of the decline or the factors named for each part.

examples|examples-t2|1.1.note: Fiscal 2023: $8.4 billion cash paid for dividends, $8.0 billion for share repurchases; February 2024 announced 7.7% quarterly cash dividend increase to $2.25 per share. Net earnings $15.11 per diluted share; buyback per-share effect not stated.
examples|examples-t2|1.1.issues: No material issues. The piece supports every number in the note: $8.4 billion in cash paid for dividends, $8.0 billion for share repurchases, the 7.7% quarterly dividend increase to $2.25 per share announced in February 2024, and diluted EPS of $15.11. The piece also never says what effect the buybacks had on per-share results, so the note is right to say so, and this answers that part of the task. Minor context the note leaves out: payouts were funded by $21.2B operating cash flow plus $2.0B debt issued and cash on hand, and net earnings were $15.1B. The task does not ask for either of these, so the note is still sufficient.

examples|examples-t2|1.6.note: Diluted EPS $15.11 in fiscal 2023 vs $16.69 in fiscal 2022; decrease driven by lower net earnings (net earnings $15,143 million vs $17,105 million), partially offset by lower diluted shares due to share repurchases.
examples|examples-t2|1.6.issues: No material issues. Every number is in the piece and correct: diluted EPS of $15.11 in fiscal 2023 vs $16.69 in fiscal 2022, and net earnings of $15,143M vs $17,105M from the ROIC table (dollars in millions). The note keeps the piece's only direct contribution to the task: share repurchases lowered diluted shares, which partly offset the EPS decline. Minor point: the piece says the decrease was "primarily driven" by lower net earnings, and the note shortens this to "driven". The net earnings figures come from the ROIC table, not the EPS paragraph, but they are the piece's own figures and are used correctly. The tax rate, the non-GAAP text and ROIC are not about shareholder returns and were rightly left out.

examples|examples-t3|1.1.note: Fiscal 2023 net sales $152.7 billion, net earnings $15.1 billion; inventory turnover 4.3 times end fiscal 2023 vs 4.2 times fiscal 2022; ROIC 36.7% vs 44.6%, down mainly on lower operating income and higher long-term debt; no gross margin detail.
examples|examples-t3|1.1.issues: No substantive issues. Every number checks against the piece: net sales $152.7B, net earnings $15.1B, inventory turnover 4.3x vs 4.2x, and ROIC 36.7% vs 44.6%, driven by lower operating income and higher long-term debt. One small imprecision: the piece says "increase in average long-term debt" and the note says "higher long-term debt". That is close enough and does not change the meaning. The note also says "no gross margin detail", which is true. It could have said the same about supply chain costs and shrink, which the piece doesn't cover either. What the piece adds to the task is the turnover improvement and the lower operating income, and the note keeps both. Nothing else in the piece bears on inventory or margins: EPS, store counts, sales per square foot, cash flow uses and the dividend increase are all left out, and that is fine.

examples|examples-t3|1.5.note: Gross profit down $1.8 billion, 3.4%, to $51.0 billion fiscal 2023; margin 33.4% vs 33.5% fiscal 2022 from price stabilization, inventory reduction/optimization, partly offset by lower supply chain costs; shrink above historical averages, easing, no significant margin impact.
examples|examples-t3|1.5.issues: No material issues. All the numbers match the piece: gross profit down $1.8B (3.4%) to $51.0B, and margin of 33.4% vs 33.5%. The causes also match: price stabilization and inventory reduction and optimization, partly offset by lower supply chain costs. The shrink points match too: still above historical averages, year-over-year pressure easing through the year, and no significant impact on margin versus fiscal 2022. Minor nuances: (1) the note drops "primarily", so the two named causes read as the only ones rather than the main ones; (2) the piece says "no significant impact" in comparison with fiscal 2022 (year over year), and the note keeps this only by implication. Leaving out the Operating Expenses (SG&A, D&A) and Interest sections is fine, because they do not bear on the task's questions about inventory, merchandise margin, supply chain or shrink. The note keeps both margin figures, so a reader can still see the drop was only about 10 bps. That is the main evidence on whether margin was under "real pressure".

examples2|examples2-t1|1.2.note: $ millions, Fiscal 2023/2022: net sales 152,669/157,403; cost of sales 101,709/104,625; gross profit 50,960/52,778; SG&A 26,598/26,284; D&A 2,673/2,455; operating income 21,689/24,039; interest income (178)/(55); interest expense 1,943/1,617; interest and other, net 1,765/1,562; shares outstanding 992/1,016.
examples2|examples2-t1|1.2.issues:
All ten number pairs in the note match the piece. Checked: net sales 152,669/157,403; cost of sales 101,709/104,625; gross profit 50,960/52,778; SG&A 26,598/26,284; D&A 2,673/2,455; operating income 21,689/24,039; interest income (178)/(55); interest expense 1,943/1,617; interest and other, net 1,765/1,562; shares outstanding 992/1,016.

Minor points, none of which change the verdict:
(1) The "$ millions" label also covers the share count, but shares are millions of shares, not dollars.
(2) The share counts are year-end outstanding shares from the balance sheet (Jan 28, 2024 / Jan 29, 2023), not weighted-average diluted shares. The note does not claim they are diluted, but calling them "Fiscal 2023/2022" hides that they come from the balance sheet.
(3) The piece's line is "Interest income and other, net". The note shortens it to "interest income".
(4) Some items are left out: total operating expenses 29,271/28,739 (you can get it by adding SG&A and D&A), the Fiscal 2021 column (not needed for the task), and the treasury share counts 804/778 with treasury stock at cost (95,372)/(87,298). The treasury figures show the buybacks behind the lower share count. The outstanding-share figures already cover the share-count driver, so this is a small loss.

The piece stops at "Interest and other, net". It has no income tax, net earnings or EPS lines, so the note cannot be faulted for leaving them out.

examples2|examples2-t1|1.3.note: Fiscal 2023 vs Fiscal 2022, in millions: earnings before income taxes 19,924 vs 22,477; income tax provision 4,781 vs 5,372; net earnings $15,143 vs $17,105; diluted shares 1,002 vs 1,025; diluted EPS $15.11 vs $16.69.
examples2|examples2-t1|1.3.issues: No material issues. All ten numbers in the note match the piece for Fiscal 2023 and Fiscal 2022: earnings before income taxes 19,924 and 22,477, provision 4,781 and 5,372, net earnings $15,143 and $17,105, diluted weighted average shares 1,002 and 1,025, diluted EPS $15.11 and $16.69. The note keeps the lower part of the earnings statement that the task needs: pre-tax earnings, income taxes, net earnings, diluted share count and diluted EPS. It leaves out basic shares (999 vs 1,022), basic EPS ($15.16 vs $16.74), the Fiscal 2021 column and the comprehensive income table. The task does not need any of these, so leaving them out is fine. Minor wording point: the heading "in millions" also covers the EPS figures, which are per-share dollars. The "$" sign makes this clear enough, so it is not a faithfulness error. The note adds no interpretation beyond the piece.

examples2|examples2-t2|1.1.note: Balance sheet: Merchandise inventories $20,976 million at January 28, 2024 and $24,886 million at January 29, 2023, amounts in millions; total current assets $29,775 million and $32,471 million.
examples2|examples2-t2|1.1.issues: No real problems. Every number is in the piece and correct: merchandise inventories are $20,976M at January 28, 2024 and $24,886M at January 29, 2023, and total current assets are $29,775M and $32,471M, with the table stated in millions. For this task, the piece only adds the year-end inventory balances, and the note has them with the right dates. Two small points: the task does not ask for total current assets, though it is in the piece and harmless. The words "amounts in millions" repeat what "$... million" already says.

examples2|examples2-t2|1.5.note: Consolidated statements of cash flows, operating activities, Changes in merchandise inventories, in millions: Fiscal 2023 4,137; Fiscal 2022 (2,830); Fiscal 2021 (5,403).
examples2|examples2-t2|1.5.issues: No issues. The piece is Home Depot's consolidated cash flow statement. Its operating activities include the row "Changes in merchandise inventories": 4,137 for Fiscal 2023, (2,830) for Fiscal 2022 and (5,403) for Fiscal 2021, in millions. The note gives these three figures correctly and keeps the parentheses. This row is the only part of the piece that bears on the task, which asks how inventory moved from year to year in the cash flow statement. None of the other rows are about inventory, so leaving them out loses nothing. The note does not name Home Depot, but the piece's heading does, so this is not a real gap.

examples2|examples2-t2|1.7.note: Cost: purchase, freight, import, sourcing/distribution operating costs, depreciation, less vendor allowances. Majority: retail method, lower of cost or market; Canada, Mexico, DCs: cost method, primarily FIFO, approximately 38%. Physical/cycle counts; shrink = counted losses plus store-specific estimates from recent shrink.
examples2|examples2-t2|1.7.issues:
Every fact and number in the note matches the piece. The cost components are right, and so is "less vendor allowances", though the piece says "certain" vendor allowances. The note correctly gives the retail method at lower of cost or market for the majority, a cost method (primarily FIFO) for about 38%, and shrink as counted losses plus store-specific interim estimates based on recent shrink results. The receivables half of the piece does not bear on the task, and the note rightly leaves it out. The piece has no year-end balances or cash-flow movement, so the note cannot be expected to have them.

Minor omissions and imprecisions:
(1) The cost-method portion is carried at lower of cost or net realizable value, not lower of cost or market. The note does not say this, so a reader could assume both portions use the same test.
(2) The piece says "certain subsidiaries, including" Canada, Mexico and the distribution centers. The note lists the three as if they were the complete set.
(3) Cost-method inventory is checked every quarter against net realizable value, and the adjustments were not material in fiscal 2023 or 2022. The note leaves this out.
(4) The retail method rests on markups, markdowns and shrink. The note leaves this out.
(5) The piece defines shrink as recorded inventory minus the physical count (swell when there is excess inventory). The note does not include this definition.
(6) Counts are taken regularly in every store and distribution center. The note does not say where or how often.
(7) Estimated shrink has historically differed from actual losses by an immaterial amount. The note leaves this out.

None of these changes the core answer. Items (1) and (7) come closest to being real losses for the valuation and shrink-estimation parts of the task.

examples2|examples2-t3|1.6.note: Cash flow tail, columns fiscal 2023, 2022, 2021: net cash used in financing (15,443), (10,993), (19,120); change in cash 1,000, 482, (5,518); year-end cash $3,760, $2,757, $2,343; interest paid 1,809, 1,449, 1,269.
examples2|examples2-t3|1.6.issues: All figures match the piece: net cash used in financing (15,443)/(10,993)/(19,120), change in cash 1,000/482/(5,518), year-end cash $3,760/$2,757/$2,343, and interest paid 1,809/1,449/1,269. Minor points: (1) The piece has no column headers. The labels "fiscal 2023, 2022, 2021" are inferred, though the inference holds: each column's beginning cash equals the next column's ending cash (2,757 and 2,343), which confirms newest-first order, and it fits the task's fiscal years. (2) The note shortens "cash paid for interest, net of interest capitalized" to "interest paid". This is harmless. (3) Some items are left out but are not needed for the task: the FX effect (3, (68), (34)), which explains why 2,757 + 1,000 does not equal 3,760; beginning-of-year cash (the 2021 opening balance of 7,895 cannot be derived from the note); income taxes paid (5,023/5,435/5,504); and non-cash capex (364/351/421). The piece has no operating, investing, dividend, buyback or borrowing lines, so the note correctly adds nothing on those. What the piece contributes is preserved: financing outflows were larger in 2023 than in 2022, and cash still grew. The notes-to-statements text (business description, consolidation, estimates, cash-equivalents definition) is not relevant and is correctly dropped.
